questions.prompt: What does OpenAI say red teaming adds to evals?

options.text: It replaces evals once a product is live
options.explanation: OpenAI says mature evaluation programs often use both.

options.text: It targets misuse and failures ordinary tests may miss
options.explanation: Right. It complements evals with adversarial cases.

options.text: It measures cost and speed per task on a fixed bank
options.explanation: That is a baseline use of evals, not red teaming.

questions.prompt: In an indirect prompt injection, who is the adversary, per the Claude docs?

options.text: The author of third-party content the model reads, while the user is trusted
options.explanation: Right. Examples are web pages, emails, documents and tool results.

options.text: The user typing into the chat, who crafts inputs to beat your rules
options.explanation: That is the direct threat model, where the user is the adversary.

options.text: The model provider, whose model may ignore your instructions
options.explanation: The docs do not describe the provider as the adversary.

questions.prompt: What makes an adversarial test different from a standard eval, per Gemini?

options.text: It needs no expected results, because any output is acceptable
options.explanation: Adversarial tests still define what a safe result is.

options.text: It runs only once, because attacks do not vary between runs
options.explanation: The guide says outputs vary, so multiple rounds may be needed.

options.text: The test data, chosen to be most likely to elicit problematic output
options.explanation: Right. The guide says the composition of the test data is what differs.
